content: The mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is a parameter included in a standard complete blood count (CBC) that measures the average size of red blood cells. In patients with anemia, the MCV value is critical for classifying the anemia as either microcytic (MCV below the normal range) or macrocytic (MCV above the normal range). The MCV can be calculated in liters by dividing the hematocrit by the red blood cell count (number of red blood cells per liter). The result is typically expressed in femtoliters (fL). When the MCV is determined using automated equipment, the result should be cross-checked with red blood cell morphology on a peripheral blood smear. Any discrepancies between the two methods may indicate either equipment malfunction or technician error. The normal reference range for MCV is generally 80–96 fL. In cases of hemolytic anemia, the presence of reticulocytes (immature red blood cells) can lead to an increased MCV. In pernicious anemia, a type of macrocytic anemia, the MCV can rise to as high as 150 fL. An elevated MCV is also associated with chronic alcohol use, often accompanied by an elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) level and an aspartate aminotransferase (AST) to alanine aminotransferase (ALT) ratio of 2:1. Vitamin B12 deficiency is another common cause of macrocytic anemia, characterized by high MCV values. The most frequent causes of microcytic anemia include iron deficiency (due to insufficient dietary intake, gastrointestinal blood loss, or menstrual blood loss), thalassemia, and anemia of chronic disease. A low MCV in a patient with a positive stool guaiac test (indicating blood in the stool) strongly suggests gastrointestinal cancer. In cases of iron deficiency anemia, the MCV can drop as low as 60–70 fL. In thalassemia, the MCV may also be low, even in the absence of iron deficiency.
